1. The animation shows a grid of tiles, apparently one per starting month, that compares buying with renting over past US history. Light tiles mean the buyer was ahead after ten years. Dark tiles mean the renter was ahead. The data sources are FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. The label "Illustrative" and the caption "US only · history, not a forecast" frame it as a look back.

2. The pattern of dark and light tiles shifts from frame to frame. The dark band is in the middle in frames 1–2. In frames 3–6, dark tiles also appear along the left edge, and the middle band narrows and moves. The "January 1991" label stays the same in every frame, so what changes is the tile pattern, not the date. The grid seems to be redrawn under a different holding assumption. In the last two frames, the text "held five years: buyer ahead in 74.4%" appears.

3. Over the historical periods shown, most starting points have light tiles. In the frames with the 74.4% label, a buyer who held the home for five years came out ahead about three-quarters of the time. The remaining roughly 26% of starting points, the dark tiles, favored renting. So buying has usually, but not always, beaten renting historically. The result depends on when you start.

4. A viewer could take away that buying tends to beat renting if they hold the home for several years, but that it is not guaranteed. The animation does not give explicit advice. It states only the 74.4% figure.

5. The advice in 4 is my own inference. The on-screen text gives the 74.4% statistic and the caveats "illustrative" and "history, not a forecast". It never tells the viewer to buy or rent, or to hold for any particular length of time.
